title: "Signal conditioning board"

This is the board tier 2 and tier 3 experiments share: whatever the sensor
is, its output has to be moved onto the ADC's actual input window before it
is worth digitizing at all. This page derives each stage from the ADC's own
limits, states the requirements a purchased part must meet, and leaves the
part number for later.

## Why conditioning at all {#sec-cond-why}

Every board in [Supported boards](../setup/boards.qmd) has an ADC with a
fixed, unipolar input range: 0 to $V_\mathrm{ref}$, where $V_\mathrm{ref}$ is
3.3 V on most supported boards and 5 V on the two Renesas ones. Nothing about
that range adapts to whatever is connected to it. A sensor's own output range
is whatever its physics gives you, and it is essentially never
$[0, V_\mathrm{ref}]$.

[S1](../experiments/S1-daq-static/index.qmd) puts a number on what that
mismatch costs. A 16-bit converter with $V_\mathrm{ref}=3.3\,$V has a
quantization step

$$
q = \frac{V_\mathrm{ref}}{2^{16}-1} \approx 50.4\ \mu\mathrm{V}
$$ {#eq-cond-lsb}

and S1 measures that its own noise floor erodes even a *full-scale*, 3.3 V
input from 16 nominal bits down to roughly 11 effective ones. Now feed the
same converter a sensor whose useful output spans only 0–50 mV — not an
unusual figure for a bridge or a low-level analog sensor (S1's own handbook
poses exactly this case). Using @eq-cond-lsb, that signal occupies

$$
\frac{50\ \mathrm{mV}}{50.4\ \mu\mathrm{V}} \approx 992\ \text{codes}
$$

out of 65535 available — under 10 bits of the nominal 16, before any noise is
even considered. Whatever effective resolution the converter has left after
its own noise, this signal starts from a worse position, because it was
never given the range to use.

::: {.callout-important}
## The fix is gain before the converter, never after

Multiplying a digitized value by a gain in software does not put back codes
that were never produced. A reading that used 992 codes still uses 992
distinct values after multiplication — only their spacing changes. The only
way to recover resolution is to make the *physical* signal occupy more of
$[0, V_\mathrm{ref}]$ before it is converted, which means gain applied in the
analog domain, ahead of the ADC.
:::

## The offset-and-scale stage {#sec-cond-offset-scale}

Given a sensor's operating range $[V_{in,\min}, V_{in,\max}]$, the
conditioning stage must implement a linear map onto the ADC input,

$$
V_\mathrm{adc} = G\,V_{in} + V_\mathrm{off}
$$ {#eq-cond-map}

Rather than mapping the sensor's range onto the whole $[0, V_\mathrm{ref}]$,
design for an interior window $[p_\mathrm{lo}V_\mathrm{ref},\,
p_\mathrm{hi}V_\mathrm{ref}]$ with $0 < p_\mathrm{lo} < p_\mathrm{hi} < 1$ —
for example $p_\mathrm{lo}=0.05$, $p_\mathrm{hi}=0.95$. Solving @eq-cond-map
at the two endpoints of the sensor's range gives

$$
G = \frac{(p_\mathrm{hi}-p_\mathrm{lo})\,V_\mathrm{ref}}{V_{in,\max}-V_{in,\min}},
\qquad
V_\mathrm{off} = p_\mathrm{lo}V_\mathrm{ref} - G\,V_{in,\min}
$$ {#eq-cond-gain-offset}

For example, mapping a $\pm 5\,$V bipolar generator output — the kind S2 and
S3 drive into the board — onto a $3.3\,$V unipolar input, with
$p_\mathrm{lo}=0.05$ and $p_\mathrm{hi}=0.95$: @eq-cond-gain-offset gives
$G = 0.9\times3.3/10 \approx 0.297$ and
$V_\mathrm{off} = 0.05\times3.3 - 0.297\times(-5) \approx 1.65\,$V. The
generator's output is attenuated *and* shifted, not merely shifted, because
its own swing already exceeds the ADC's.

Three reasons to leave headroom instead of using the full $0$–$100\,\%$:

1. **Overshoot.** A real signal is rarely bounded exactly by its nominal
   range — noise, a transient, a slightly-out-of-spec calibration source —
   and a signal that saturates a rail produces a hard, easily-missed
   nonlinearity (clipping) instead of a value that is merely close to a
   limit.
2. **Op-amp output swing.** Few op-amps swing all the way to their supply
   rails; even "rail-to-rail" parts have a dropout of some tens of
   millivolts near each rail, so a design that targets 0 V or
   $V_\mathrm{ref}$ exactly is targeting a region the amplifier may not
   reach linearly.
3. **A calibration needs both ends free.** Fitting @eq-cond-map — or a small
   nonlinearity around it — needs points that bracket the operating range;
   leaving margin means an out-of-range calibration point does not itself
   clip.

## Resistive dividers {#sec-cond-dividers}

The simplest way to move a voltage down is a two-resistor divider:

$$
V_\mathrm{adc} = V_{in}\,\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2} = V_{in}\,D,
\qquad D=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}
$$ {#eq-cond-divider}

### Loading

The divider's Thévenin source resistance, as seen by the ADC, is
$R_s = R_1 \parallel R_2$. The ADC's sample-and-hold capacitor
$C_\mathrm{sh}$ must charge through $R_s$ within the sampling time
$t_\mathrm{acq}$ the board allows per conversion. Settling to within one
half-LSB after a step takes roughly $n\ln 2$ time constants for an $n$-bit
converter, so

$$
t_\mathrm{acq} \;\ge\; R_s\,C_\mathrm{sh}\,n\ln 2
$$ {#eq-cond-settle}

[@kester2005]. A divider built from resistors large enough to draw
negligible current from the sensor can easily be too large to satisfy
@eq-cond-settle — which is the usual reason a divider needs a buffer behind
it (@sec-cond-buffer) rather than feeding the ADC directly.

### Tolerance and temperature coefficient

$D$ in @eq-cond-divider is a function of two resistors, each known only to
its tolerance. For $R_i$ with relative tolerance $\delta_i$ treated as a
rectangular bound, $u(R_i) = R_i\delta_i/\sqrt{3}$, and the sensitivity
coefficients are

$$
\frac{\partial D}{\partial R_1} = -\frac{D}{R_1+R_2},
\qquad
\frac{\partial D}{\partial R_2} = \frac{1-D}{R_1+R_2}
$$ {#eq-cond-div-sens}

so that, combining independently,

$$
u(D) = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\partial D}{\partial R_1}u(R_1)\right)^2 +
             \left(\frac{\partial D}{\partial R_2}u(R_2)\right)^2}
$$ {#eq-cond-div-u}

If the two resistors are drawn from the same reel and share a temperature
coefficient $\alpha$, a uniform temperature change $\Delta T$ scales both by
$(1+\alpha\Delta T)$ and $D$ is unchanged — a ratio is what a divider
measures, and matched TCs cancel in it. What does not cancel is any
*mismatch* $\Delta\alpha = \alpha_1-\alpha_2$ between the two parts, which
contributes an additional drift of order $D(1-D)\,\Delta\alpha\,\Delta T$ to
the ratio. A matched pair, or a single resistor network on one substrate,
removes this term almost entirely; two resistors from different batches do
not.

### Why a divider alone cannot give gain

$D=R_2/(R_1+R_2)<1$ for any positive $R_1,R_2$: a purely resistive divider
can only attenuate. Producing $G>1$ needs an active stage, which is the
subject of the next two sections.

## The instrumentation amplifier {#sec-cond-inamp}

A bridge — a load cell, a strain-gauge bridge on the [beam
rig](beam-rig.qmd) — does not present a voltage referenced to ground: it
presents a small *differential* voltage between two nodes that each sit near
half the excitation voltage, common mode. A single-ended amplifier measures
one node relative to ground and cannot separate the differential signal from
that common-mode level without amplifying the common-mode level's own noise
and drift by the same gain. An instrumentation amplifier is built to reject
exactly that [@doebelin]:

$$
V_\mathrm{out} = G\left(V_+ - V_-\right) + \text{(rejected common mode)}
$$

quantified by its common-mode rejection ratio,

$$
\mathrm{CMRR} = 20\log_{10}\frac{A_d}{A_\mathrm{cm}}
$$ {#eq-cond-cmrr}

A common-mode voltage $V_\mathrm{cm}$ appears at the output as an equivalent
differential error of $V_\mathrm{cm}/\mathrm{CMRR}$ (the linear ratio, not
the dB figure) referred to the input — for a bridge sitting at several volts
of common mode and a differential signal of millivolts, CMRR is not a
footnote, it is the reason this stage exists at all.

**Input bias current.** Every real amplifier input draws a small bias
current $I_B$. Through a source impedance $R_s$ that current produces an
offset $I_B R_s$, and through *mismatched* impedances at the two inputs, an
offset current $I_\mathrm{os}$ produces a differential error
$I_\mathrm{os}\,\Delta R_s$. For a low-impedance bridge (hundreds of ohms)
this is usually negligible; for a high-impedance source it is not, and it is
one more reason to buffer a high-impedance sensor (@sec-cond-buffer) before,
not instead of, amplifying it.

::: {.callout-note}
## Requirements for the in-amp — part left open

A suitable device must be:

- single-supply, since the board provides no negative rail;
- rail-to-rail output, or with enough headroom that @eq-cond-gain-offset's
  window is reachable;
- specified with an input offset voltage and drift small compared with the
  smallest signal to be resolved;
- gain-settable by a single external resistor, so $G$ in
  @eq-cond-gain-offset is chosen once the sensor's range is known.

The part itself is [TODO (Paolo)]{.todo}.
:::

## The buffer {#sec-cond-buffer}

A high-impedance source — the output of a divider sized for low current
draw, a piezoresistive or capacitive sensor — cannot itself satisfy
@eq-cond-settle at a reasonable acquisition time. A unity-gain op-amp
follower between the source and the ADC solves this: its own output
impedance is set by open-loop gain and feedback, not by the source, and is
small enough that a deliberately added series $R_\mathrm{filt}$ and shunt
$C_\mathrm{filt}$ at the ADC pin — which double as ESD protection and a
first noise-bandwidth limit — can be sized directly from @eq-cond-settle
with $R_s \to R_\mathrm{filt}$:

$$
R_\mathrm{filt}C_\mathrm{filt} \le \frac{t_\mathrm{acq}}{n\ln 2}
$$ {#eq-cond-buf-rc}

with no dependence on the sensor's own, now-buffered, impedance.

## What goes in the sidecar {#sec-cond-sidecar}

The [`conditioning` block](../data-format/index.qmd#sec-fields) of every
channel carries `gain` and `offset`. These must be the **fitted** values
from a calibration against a reference — applying known inputs at the
sensor connector and fitting @eq-cond-map to the ADC readings — never the
values computed from @eq-cond-gain-offset with nominal resistor and
gain-resistor values.

The reason is @eq-cond-div-u again, compounded across stages: a divider, an
in-amp gain resistor and a buffer's own gain error each contribute a
percent-level term from tolerance alone, and they do not cancel between
stages — they add. A "design" gain of, say, $G=20.0$ computed from nominal
parts can easily be the true gain to only $1$–$2\,\%$, which is worse than
the effective resolution S1 measures for the bare converter. Recording the
design value in the sidecar would silently reintroduce the very error this
board exists to remove. Calibrate the stage the same way S1 calibrates the
bare ADC — apply known references at the sensor input, fit, and record what
was fitted, not what was designed.

## Uncertainty this stage adds {#sec-cond-budget}

Write the corrected sensor value recovered from an ADC reading as

$$
\hat V_\mathrm{sensor} = \frac{V_\mathrm{adc} - V_\mathrm{off,fit}}{G_\mathrm{fit}}
$$ {#eq-cond-correct}

with sensitivity coefficients

$$
\frac{\partial \hat V_\mathrm{sensor}}{\partial V_\mathrm{off,fit}} = -\frac{1}{G_\mathrm{fit}},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat V_\mathrm{sensor}}{\partial G_\mathrm{fit}} =
  -\frac{V_\mathrm{adc}-V_\mathrm{off,fit}}{G_\mathrm{fit}^2} =
  -\frac{\hat V_\mathrm{sensor}}{G_\mathrm{fit}}
$$ {#eq-cond-sens}

Three components an experiment using this board should carry into its own
budget, following [Data format](../data-format/index.qmd#sec-budget):

| Component | Nature | Sensitivity | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gain uncertainty $u(G_\mathrm{fit})$ | Multiplicative | $\propto \hat V_\mathrm{sensor}$ | Standard error of the calibration fit |
| Offset uncertainty $u(V_\mathrm{off,fit})$ | Additive | Constant, $1/G_\mathrm{fit}$ | Standard error of the calibration fit |
| Drift with temperature | Influence quantity | Via $\partial G/\partial T$, $\partial V_\mathrm{off}/\partial T$ | Component temperature coefficients and the bench's $\Delta T$ from calibration |

: Uncertainty components contributed by the conditioning board {#tbl-cond-budget}

The distinction in the second column matters when reading a budget: a gain
error scales with how large the reading is, so it dominates near full scale;
an offset error is the same absolute size everywhere in the range, so it
dominates near zero. A budget that only reports $u_c$ at one operating point
hides which of the two is actually being seen.
